newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma poised to name PM after IMF blow.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma poised to name PM after IMF blow.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma looked poised on Friday to name his candidate for prime minister after an up-and-down week for his economically troubled former Soviet republic.

He returned victorious from sealing a security pact with NATO in Madrid but then the International Monetary Fund decided to delay a long-term loan because it felt Kiev's economic reforms were not moving fast enough.
Ukraine seemed determined to take the blow with dignity, saying reforms would continue anyway.
The IMF, whose mission to Kiev ended on Thursday, said it would come back later with an offer of a standby credit to see Ukraine through the pain of implementing structural reforms.
"Ukraine expected compliance no matter what half-hearted efforts they made," a Western economist said on Friday.
"The standby is better than nothing. It's a qualified gesture of confidence in Ukraine," he added.
Instead of a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion loan, Ukraine was told it might get a smaller interim deal, with the bigger cash coming late this year or in early 1998.
Analysts said they expected Kuchma to start ruling more by decree after years of fighting to push reforms through a 450-seat, conservative-dominated parliament.

He has picked a new fight with deputies by pressing for an extension of their term by a year from March 1998 in a move designed to make them accept responsibility for painful reforms. But he needs the support of 301 deputies to win the extension.
The tussle already lost him one key reformer, Viktor Pynzenyk, who resigned in April disgusted with the attitude of government and parliament.

Even Pynzenyk's youthful replacement as deputy prime minister overseeing reforms, Serhiy Tyhypko, who said when he was appointed that everything would be fine if everyone worked together, seemed to be running out of patience.
"Don't torment me now about the standby," said Tyhypko, who has been trying to push through last-minute laws as parliament prepares to go into recess on July 18.
"We did so much recently to extract the EFF and each time we did something, we devised, we schemed and we didn't get it through parliament," he said.
Kuchma, whose reform-shy prime minister Pavlo Lazarenko resigned on grounds of health -- though few believe he was actually ill -- said on Thursday he could name a replacement within days.

He added the deal with NATO, which promises Ukraine consultations if it feels threatened, would also provide economic benefits. "I believe it to be a sort of protection for foreign investment from the NATO member states as well."
Kuchma was due to hold consultations with parliamentary representatives on Friday and Saturday. He hopes to propose a new prime minister before the parliamentary recess.
The constitution says 226 deputies must approve the candidate for prime minister, whose duties are being carried out by acting premier Vasyl Durdynets.

The two potential candidates most often mentioned in parliament are Ivan Plyushch, 55, a centrist deputy and former speaker known for his sharp wit, and Valery Pustovoitenko, 50, minister without portfolio who also heads the former Soviet republic's football federation.
Pustovoitenko ran Kuchma's election campaign office in 1994, and the respected Den daily said this could signal the start of Kuchma's next election campaign for October 1999.
